b: Most revenue leaders don’t want another tool. They want their existing tools to talk to each other. In HubSpot’s 2026 State of Sales report, 88% of revenue and sales leaders agreed their sales process would benefit from a single, integrated platform, and few companies get there by buying one. Most build an integrated CRM system out of the tools they already run.

CRM software integrations are the connections that make that possible: A marketing platform that passes a new lead to the CRM; a support desk that logs a ticket for the same contact; a billing tool that marks the deal as paid. The result is shared context. Reps see the campaign that produced a lead before the first call, and support agents see the open renewal before answering a ticket.

Choosing CRM software integrations well comes down to three questions: Which connection model fits best (native, iPaaS, API, or two-way sync), which tools need to be connected first, and who maintains each connection once it’s live. This guide covers all three, plus where AI assistants now fit alongside a connected CRM.

Choosing CRM Integrations That Hold Up

CRM software integrations connect a CRM with the tools a business uses for marketing, sales, service, commerce, finance, and analytics, so a record created in one system appears in the others. CRM integration can run through a connector built by the CRM vendor, a middleware platform, a custom API link, or a two-way sync that keeps the two systems in sync. Whatever the method, the goal is one customer record that every team reads from and writes to.

CRM integration tools solve the silo problem: Every disconnected tool holds its own version of the customer. The marketing platform knows which emails a contact opened. The support desk knows what broke. The billing tool knows what the customer paid. When those systems don’t share records, each team works from a partial view, and the CRM retains the version someone last typed.

A connected system eliminates those gaps with a single record, unifying customer context across marketing, sales, and service workflows, so every hub reads the same contact, company, and deal records.
Across revenue teams, integrations improve three things:

Visibility. Activity from every connected tool lands on the CRM record. When a deal shows the webinar a contact attended, the ticket they opened last month, and outstanding invoices, reps have more context than any single system.

Automation. Triggers can cross tool boundaries. In an integrated system like HubSpot’s Smart CRM, a form submission on the website can automatically create a contact, assign an owner, and enroll that contact in a follow-up sequence without anyone having to touch the record. HubSpot Marketing Hub workflows and Sales Hub sequences both run on CRM data, so a trigger in one hub can start an action in the other.

Handoffs. The record travels with the customer. When marketing qualifies a lead, the rep inherits the full engagement history. When a deal closes, onboarding sees the terms and the commitments made during the sale. When a ticket surfaces an upsell, service can flag it to the account owner. None of it requires a forwarded email or a re-entered record.
How to Choose a CRM Integration Model
A CRM integration model is the method used to connect the CRM with another system. The four most common CRM integration models are:
Native integration built by the CRM vendor.
iPaaS tool that sits between systems.
Two-way sync that keeps records matched in both directions.
The right model depends on how standard the use case is, who will maintain the connection, and how much control the business needs over what moves and when.

In HubSpot’s 2026 State of Sales report, 65% of revenue teams spend two to 10 hours per month maintaining integrations, a cost most evaluations leave out. If a model takes an afternoon to set up, that can cost a day per month for as long as it runs.

The table below compares the four models on setup speed, technical complexity, control over the data flow, and ongoing maintenance, with the situation each one suits best. Setup timelines follow HubSpot’s guide to CRM integration. The other columns describe typical tradeoffs.
Pros and Cons of CRM Integration Models
Native CRM integrations are prebuilt connections that the CRM vendor or its partners maintain and install from an app marketplace with little or no configuration.

Native integrations reduce setup time and ongoing maintenance for common use cases because the vendor handles version changes on both sides. HubSpot’s App Marketplace is one example. Connections to email, calendar, meeting, and messaging tools install in a few clicks and update without the customer’s involvement.

A native integration moves only the fields and objects that the vendor supports. A business that needs a custom object synced, or a field mapped in a way the connector doesn’t offer, will hit the ceiling quickly.

Integration platform as a service (iPaaS) tools such as Zapier, Make, Workato, and Boomi connect systems through a hosted middle layer, where users build a flow that watches for a trigger in one app and performs an action in another.

iPaaS tools help businesses connect systems when native integrations fall short, whether because no native connector exists or the connection needs conditional logic, multi-step routing, or a transformation between the two data models.
Operations teams often reach for these CRM integration tools first, and iPaaS vendors range from no-code consumer tools to enterprise platforms with built-in governance and monitoring.

iPaaS comes with two costs: A subscription billed per task or per flow, and a second place where logic lives outside the CRM. When a connected app renames or removes a field, the flow stops at that step, and someone has to notice.

An API integration is custom code that calls the CRM’s application programming interface directly, written and maintained by the business’s own engineers or an agency. It offers full control over what data moves, how it’s transformed, and when the call runs, and it’s the only option for systems with no connector on any platform.

API rate limits, authentication changes, and schema updates on either side all land on the team that wrote the code. API integrations make sense for high-volume data flows, proprietary systems, and data models that a prebuilt connector can’t represent. Still, they make less sense for anything a native integration already covers.

Two-way sync keeps records matched in both systems, so a change in either one updates the other. It’s a behavior more than a method — native integrations, iPaaS flows, and API code can all implement it. The difference from a one-way push is that both systems act as sources of truth, which means the integration must decide what happens when they disagree.

Two-way sync suits pairs of systems that both need up-to-date data, such as a CRM and an enterprise resource planning (ERP) system, or a CRM and a support desk. It also carries the highest governance load of the four models, because duplicates, field conflicts, and stale data compound in both directions.
The CRM Software Integrations Most Revenue Teams Evaluate First

Six categories of CRM software integrations come up in almost every evaluation: marketing automation, sales enablement, customer service, commerce and ERP, analytics and business intelligence (BI), and collaboration tools. Each one connects a different stage of the customer relationship to the CRM record, and the order a business tackles them usually follows where the data gaps hurt most.

Marketing automation integrations pass leads, form submissions, email engagement, and campaign membership into the CRM, and push CRM data back out to drive segmentation. CRM website integration is usually the first piece. Forms, chat, and page tracking feed new contacts into the CRM with the source attached, so a rep knows what a lead read before the first conversation.

When campaign and deal data live on the same record, marketing can report on pipeline and revenue rather than clicks and opens. In HubSpot, Marketing Hub runs on the same records as the CRM, and its campaigns tool ties every campaign asset to the contacts and deals it influences. Marketing automation workflows then trigger follow-up from CRM properties, such as a lifecycle stage change or a form fill, without a separate sync.
Sales enablement integrations bring the tools a rep uses during the sale into the CRM, so the record updates itself. The ones to connect first:
Email and calendar, so every sent message and booked meeting logs in the contact.
Call and meeting recording, so the conversation is attached to the deal.
E-signature, quoting, and prospecting data, so a signed proposal moves the stage, and a new lead arrives with context.

Without those connections, activity capture depends on reps typing it in, and that often doesn’t happen. Sales Hub natively covers email tracking, meeting scheduling, and calling. Its sales automation tools can enroll an existing contact in a follow-up sequence when a CRM property changes, so the next touch happens on schedule.
For tools outside the platform, the App Marketplace carries connectors for most e-signature, quoting, and conversation intelligence vendors.

Customer service integrations connect the help desk, live chat, knowledge base, and survey tools to the CRM, so a ticket appears on the same record as the preceding deal. For a revenue team, the point is retention. A rep preparing a renewal conversation needs to know about the three open tickets before the customer brings them up.

Support teams need account context from sales (contract value, renewal date, owner), and sales needs support history, so this integration usually runs both ways. Service Hub handles this on the same platform. Zendesk and Intercom connect the same way through native integrations.

Commerce and ERP integrations sync orders, invoices, payments, inventory, and account balances between the CRM and the back-office systems. Ecommerce CRM integration connects an online store so that purchase history is captured on the contact record. An ERP and CRM integration does the same for invoicing, fulfillment, and financials.

The ERP is often the system of record for the customer’s legal entity and billing details, and the CRM is the system of record for the relationship, so a field conflict between the two can produce an incorrect invoice. HubSpot’s Revenue Hub brings quoting, billing, and payments into the CRM natively, and connectors to NetSuite, QuickBooks, Shopify, and Stripe cover the systems most businesses already run.

Analytics and BI integrations pull CRM data into a data warehouse or reporting tool such as Looker, Tableau, or Power BI, where it can be joined with product usage, finance, and marketing data the CRM doesn’t hold. A revenue leader needs data from more than one system in the same query to see win rate by acquisition channel or churn by onboarding path.

This integration usually runs one way, CRM out, which makes it lower-risk than a sync. The decision is how fresh the data needs to be, and a nightly export is enough for most reporting. HubSpot’s own dashboard and reporting software covers the CRM-only view, and data warehouse connectors handle the joins.

Collaboration integrations push CRM events into the tools where a team already talks: A deal-stage change posts to a Slack channel, a new lead assignment creates a task in Asana, and a meeting booked in the CRM lands on a Google or Outlook calendar. The record doesn’t change, but who sees it does.

These are the fastest integrations to justify because they cost almost nothing and remove the “Did anyone see this?” problem. Sales Hub works with Gmail, Google Workspace, Outlook, and Office 365 for email and calendar, and HubSpot’s Slack and Teams connectors cover notifications. Every channel a notification goes to adds another place that needs a rule for when it fires.
How to Keep CRM Sync and Data Quality Under Control
Two-way CRM sync requires governance to prevent duplicates, field conflicts, and bad data. That governance comes down to four controls:

Field mapping. A field map is the written record of which field in system A writes to which field in system B, in which direction, and what happens on conflict. It has to cover format (a date stored as text in one system and as a date in the other will fail silently), picklist values (a “Closed Won” stage in the CRM has to map to a specific status in the ERP), and the rule for disagreement (most recent write wins, one system always wins, or the sync stops and flags). Undocumented maps are the usual source of a field that “used to sync.” Someone renamed a property, and the integration kept running with nothing to write to.

Testing. Every integration change gets tested against a copy of production data before it touches live records. HubSpot Enterprise accounts include a sandbox for this. Elsewhere, a filtered test list does the same job. The test must include failure cases: a missing required field, a duplicate email, and a value the picklist doesn’t recognize.

Permissions. An integration should have the narrowest set of permissions that lets it do its job. A connector that only needs to read deals gets no write access to contacts. Scoped permissions limit the damage from a misconfigured flow and keep the audit trail readable.

Ownership. Each integration has one named person who gets the error notifications, approves changes to the field map, and reviews the sync logs on a schedule. Shared ownership is no ownership. The owner doesn’t have to be technical, only accountable.
A one-way push can survive without all four. A sync that writes in both directions cannot, because every error it makes gets copied back to the source.

Reconciliation time is the cost of skipping these controls. In HubSpot’s 2026 State of Sales report, 43% of teams spend six to 10 hours per month reconciling revenue data, which is roughly a business day lost to finding out why two systems disagree.

A CRM data integration strategy that settles the map, the tests, and the owner before launch turns that day back into selling time. In HubSpot, Data Hub is the platform’s data management software, and it’s where field definitions and data-quality tooling live for a business running the CRM as its system of record.
Where AI Fits in CRM Software Integrations

AI tools fit into a CRM stack as a layer that reads the CRM’s context and works through the CRM’s existing permissions. AI-assisted CRM workflows depend on those permissions, as well as on trustworthy data and human review before anything is written back.

When an AI assistant can see a contact’s engagement history, open deals, and the tickets logged this quarter, they can answer questions a rep would otherwise have to assemble by hand: Which deals have gone quiet, what happened on the last three calls with this company, which accounts have a renewal, and an open ticket at the same time.

In HubSpot’s 2026 State of Sales report, 94% of sales leaders actively use AI, while 80% say it’s “fully integrated” with their CRM. The same report found that 31% of leaders say integrating with existing systems and workflows is a major challenge in AI implementation, and its own read is that the gap between usage and integration is where ROI disappears. An AI assistant without CRM access is a very capable tool but knows nothing about the business.

An AI tool that belongs in a CRM stack inherits the user’s permissions, so a rep sees their own pipeline and an admin sees the account. It proposes actions for approval rather than taking them silently, so a deal-stage update or a logged call is something a person has confirmed. The CRM stays the system of record. The assistant is a way to ask it questions and hand it work.
The HubSpot connector for Claude gives users access to HubSpot context in Claude, so questions about contacts, deals, tickets, and engagement history get answered from the business’s own records.

A sales rep can ask for a summary of active deals sorted by close date, a pre-call brief built from the last month of emails and meetings with a contact, or a list of accounts with an upcoming renewal and an open ticket.
Customer success and support teams can compare resolution approaches across channels or pull open tickets by priority.

The connector can also create and update records, log calls, meetings, notes, and tasks, and create follow-up tasks, with the proposed change shown for approval before it’s made. It cannot delete anything.

HubSpot’s audit log records every create and update, attributed to both the user and the connector. The connector also inherits each user’s HubSpot permissions, so a rep sees the same records in Claude as they do in HubSpot. Sensitive Data properties are not available to it.

The connector works with any HubSpot account, including the free tier, and requires a paid Claude plan. A Super Admin enables it once for the account and chooses what it can access. After that, each user connects individually. Setup steps and the full list of supported records are on the HubSpot connector for Claude page.

HubSpot’s own AI runs inside the platform through Agent Hub, where agents work on the same records natively. The connector is for the other case: A team that already does its thinking in Claude and wants that thinking grounded in what HubSpot knows.
Common CRM Integration Mistakes to Avoid

Four mistakes account for most CRM integration failures: Duplicate records created by overlapping sources, brittle logic that breaks on the first unexpected value, unclear ownership that leaves errors unread, and automation built on data that hasn’t been cleaned.
Each one is cheap to prevent at setup but expensive to unwind after a few months of running.

Duplicates happen when two or more tools create records in the CRM without agreeing on how to identify an existing one. A form tool matches on email, an event platform matches on name, and a billing system matches on nothing, creating a new contact every time. Within a quarter, the CRM has three versions of the same customer, each with part of the history.

The fix is one matching rule that every integration follows. Email is the usual key for contacts and domain for companies, with a fallback for records that lack one. Any integration that can’t apply the rule should create records in a holding list for review, instead of writing straight to the database.

Brittle logic is an integration that works only when the data looks exactly the way it did during setup. The examples are familiar to anyone who has run one. A flow that fails because a rep left the deal amount blank; a picklist mapping that stops working after someone renames a label; or a workflow that assumes one contact per company and breaks when a second one is added. In each case, the integration passed its tests, and the tests used clean records.
Integration logic has to assume the data will be incomplete and inconsistent, because it will be. Three setup choices cover most of it:
Map picklists by internal value, not by display label.
Treat every field as optional unless the source system enforces it.
Send any record the logic can’t handle to an exception list and notify the owner. A failed record then becomes a task instead of a silent skip.

Unclear ownership is an integration with no named person responsible for its errors, changes, or logs. That integration can fail for weeks before anyone notices, because the notifications go to a shared inbox or to someone who set it up and has since changed roles. When a person finally investigates, the damage is done to every record the integration touched or skipped in the interim.
Naming an owner at setup, then reassigning that name when people move, costs nothing and is the one control that shortens the time between a failure and its discovery.
Over-Automating Before the Data Is Clean

Over-automating is turning on lead routing, reminders, or AI-driven actions before the data those automations depend on has been audited and cleaned. Automation built on unclean data does the wrong thing faster.

For example: A lead-routing workflow that assigns by territory sends every lead with a blank country field to the wrong rep, at scale. Or, a renewal reminder keyed to a contract date that’s populated on half the accounts misses the other half. An AI assistant asked to flag stale deals returns a list that reflects the CRM’s data gaps as much as its pipeline.

Data cleanup comes first, then the integrations, then the automations that run on them. Running a data audit before the first integration goes live (required fields, duplicate rate, picklist consistency, orphaned records) establishes what the automation can rely on. Anything the audit shows as unreliable stays manual until it’s fixed. In HubSpot, Data Hub is where that audit and ongoing quality work live, and Smart CRM is the single record the automations run on.

Choosing CRM Integrations That Hold Up

A CRM integration holds up when the model matches the job (native for common tools, iPaaS for logic and gaps, API for custom systems, two-way sync only where both sides are a system of record), when the field map, test plan, and owner exist before the first record moves, and when automation waits for the data audit. Most integration failures trace back to skipping one of those steps.

The fewer separate systems a business has to connect, the fewer of those steps it has to get right. HubSpot’s Smart CRM runs marketing, sales, service, and commerce on one set of records, so the remaining integrations are to outside tools, each with a native connector or a documented map. For a business whose reps and managers already work in Claude, the HubSpot connector for Claude brings contacts, deals, and engagement history into Claude while preserving HubSpot permissions.
